title: Building the YN notebook
summary: How I turned a monthly study archive into a home for essays, project notes, and study logs, with clearer navigation and shorter paths to the writing.

coverImage.alt: The website homepage with its amber I learn by building headline, Currently panel, and Writing, Projects, Progress, About navigation.

children.text: The notebook grew out of a monthly study archive. That format was good for looking back over a month, but it gave an essay and a practical project the same place and presentation. I wanted each kind of work to be easier to recognize and find.

I set out to give the essays, projects, and study logs distinct homes while keeping the notebook personal. The homepage now leads to a piece of writing, and the Progress archive opens with the logs. The typography gives interface labels and long paragraphs different jobs.

Next.js renders the content on the server. Sanity remains an optional editor, with local JSON files available for direct editing in VS Code. Rich text preserves headings, links, lists, images, code, tables, and mathematics.

The older essays and study logs were stored as projects. Reclassifying the pages without breaking links meant keeping the original records and their section anchors, then redirecting the old URLs. On smaller screens, the reading layout also needed to make the contents available before a large cover image.

A reader can now open the latest essay from the homepage, jump directly to a section on a phone, or find the monthly notes under Progress. The site has a shared reading layout and keeps the original URLs working through redirects.
Content models are part of the reading experience. A project needs room for process and outcomes; a progress log needs room for reflection; an essay needs room to develop an argument.
